extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics and mathematicians interested in methodology, history and foundations of mathematical practice
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing and improving informal mathematical proofs and conjectures using Lakatos's 'proofs and refutations' methodology: use of counterexamples, hidden lemmas, analysis-synthesis, and heuristic research programmes to guide discovery and revision. Also assessing the relation between informal mathematics and formalisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofs as heuristic devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs are not merely devices for establishing mathematical results; centrally, proofs play a heuristic role by improving mathematical knowledge and guiding the development of conjectures and theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use proofs to generate improvements to conjectures, to reveal hidden premises/lemmas, and to direct further mathematical investigation rather than treating proofs solely as final certificates of truth. (Textual exemplars: Lakatos's claim that proofs can 'use proofs ... to improve our mathematical guesses'.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal proofs are quasi-formal, not mere 'gaps'
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'informal proof' should not be dismissed as just a formal proof with gaps; it is often a quasi-formal, pedagogically and heuristically significant form of reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat informal proofs as legitimate stages of mathematical practice that may embody discovery-methods and heuristics; avoid the anti-pattern of reducing them to childish or merely incomplete formal proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of counterexamples (local / global / local+global)
rubrics_metrics.description: Counterexamples come in three kinds — local, global but not local, and both local and global — and each kind affects whether and how the conjecture or its premises are to be revised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which kind of counterexample you have: a local counterexample refutes a premise and suggests replacing that premise; a global-but-not-local counterexample may demand strengthening antecedent conditions or adding lemmas; a counterexample that is both may require deeper reformulation. (Lakatos's taxonomy: pp. 28–31 references.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use counterexamples to identify hidden lemmas/conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Counterexamples, together with the proof, help interpret proofs by pointing to hidden conditions (lemmas) that must be made explicit for the theorem to hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a counterexample arises, search the proof for tacit assumptions or hidden lemmas that the counterexample exploits; make those assumptions explicit and add them as conditions to the theorem rather than merely discarding the theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directive 1 of proofs-and-refutations: make premises explicit / neutralize counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with a conjecture that seems to follow from some (perhaps implicit) premises; search for explicit premises and for counterexamples that are not counterexamples to those premises; replace refuted premises and add hidden lemmas as conditions so the proof becomes more rigorous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct explicit premises by analysis-synthesis, build proofs that neutralize unrefuted counterexamples by adding assumptions/lemmas, and thereby render the proof more rigorous (example: making a lemma explicit that the original argument relied upon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Directive 2 of proofs-and-refutations: analyze counterexamples to reformulate/generalize
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct counterexamples and analyze which properties they lack relative to objects where the proof does apply; reformulate the conjecture (introduce parameters, strengthen hypotheses, or generalize) so that the theorem covers intended cases and/or a more general correct statement is found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use counterexamples as information about the domain and properties to be captured; introduce new parameters or reformulate the class of objects under discussion to obtain either a corrected theorem or a more general result, then reapply Directive 1 to the new conjecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis–synthesis as a method of discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery may proceed by analysis (starting from accepted premises to deduce consequences) and synthesis (working from a conjecture backwards to infer needed premises and auxiliary assumptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use analysis to uncover consequences and lemmas, and synthesis to search for auxiliary assumptions (Qi's) that would allow deriving the conjecture; iterate analysis and synthesis to improve conjectures and proofs (Lakatos relates this to historical methods such as Pappus's).

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic rules are articulable but not mechanical
rubrics_metrics.description: Heuristic methods consist of general rules that can guide mathematical discovery but they are fallible and not mechanically applicable; they provide rational guidance rather than infallible algorithmic procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articulate heuristic rules to guide research within a programme, but recognize their dependence on human judgment and contextual application; avoid claiming they constitute algorithmic decision procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic research programme as evaluative framework
rubrics_metrics.description: A research programme's heuristics guide construction of conjectures/theories and provide narrower rules governing practice within a theoretical framework; these heuristics can explain historical mathematical procedures and successes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating mathematical practice, consider the programme of heuristics mathematicians adopt (what problems they set out to solve, what methods they consider legitimate) and how these heuristics structure growth of the theory (Lakatosian explanatory role).

rubrics_metrics.name: Material adequacy / faithful formalisation constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: A formal theory should be a faithful formalisation of the informal theory: material adequacy requires that the formalisation preserves the results and intuitions of the informal theory; if a formal theorem contradicts the corresponding heuristic/informal theorem, the formal theory may be judged 'refuted'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When accepting a formalisation of informal mathematics, check that the formal theory respects the intuitive/heuristic theorems it aims to capture; mismatches are legitimate grounds for rejecting or revising the formalisation (example: first-order formulations that negate heuristic theorems).

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation must preserve meanings — watch limits of formalisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Translating informal/mathematical-intuitive claims into formal language must preserve the relevant meanings and intuitive content; failure of translation leaves methodological issues unresolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious when translating concepts (e.g., polyhedron, continuity) into formal terms; assess whether the translation changes the intended domain or strips relevant informal content, and recognize that some debates (e.g., Euler characteristic cases) remain inconclusive when translation is dubious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not accept arbitrary 'concept-stretching' — require mathematical significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Expanding or 'stretching' the meanings of descriptive terms (e.g., 'polyhedron') is not illegitimate in itself, but it must be judged by whether such stretching leads to significant, interesting mathematical growth rather than to vacuous proliferations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid arbitrary expansions of term meanings that produce only trivial or silly classes; prefer reformulations that generate substantial new conjectures, results, or explanatory power. There is no general formal rule; assess by mathematical fruitfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish essential vs accidental events in rational reconstructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Rational (heuristic) reconstructions of historical mathematical development should focus on events essential to understanding the conceptual development and may omit accidental errors that do not bear on the pedagogic aim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For pedagogical or explanatory reconstructions, omit irrelevant accidental details; nevertheless, distinguish such pedagogic reconstructions from claims about literal historical accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate responses to different counterexample patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Different counterexample patterns call for different methodological moves: replace refuted premises, add lemmas, strengthen antecedents, restrict domain, introduce parameters, or generalise to a new correct theorem depending on whether the counterexample is local, global, or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a counterexample appears, diagnose which part of the conjecture/proof it attacks and choose the least ad hoc but mathematically fruitful repair (e.g., add hidden lemma if the proof implicitly used it; restrict domain only if that reflects intended applicability). Examples: Cauchy/Seidel in analysis, Euler characteristic adjustments for polyhedra.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic methods justify pedagogical reconstructions, not literal historicism
rubrics_metrics.description: The dialogue-style reconstructions (as in Proofs and Refutations) are meant to mirror the dialectic and to be pedagogically illuminating; they need not claim literal, one-track historical truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rational reconstructions as tools to expose heuristic structure and dialectic of theory development; accept that actual history may diverge in particulars and that multiple reconstructions may be possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject narrow identification of mathematics with formalism
rubrics_metrics.description: One should not identify mathematics merely with its formalised presentation; formal and informal mathematical activities can coexist and each contributes different insights (formalism alone does not capture heuristic discovery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating mathematical practice, allow for coexistence of informal heuristic methods and formal metamathematical study; do not dismiss informal methods as unscientific merely because they lack immediate formalisation.
